title: Is there a safe harbor for Section 174 R&D expenses?
description: There is no blanket safe harbor for Section 174 R&D expenses, but layered relief applies, including Notices 2023-63 and 2024-12 and Section 174A expensing.
summary: Is there a safe harbor for Section 174 R&D expenses? Not a single blanket exemption: U.S. federal tax law offers layered relief, including interim reliance rules in Notices 2023-63 and 2024-12, automatic accounting method changes, new Section 174A domestic expensing, and retroactive elections letting small businesses with average gross receipts up to $31 million unwind 2022–2024 capitalization.

body.text: Is there a safe harbor for Section 174 R&D expenses? Not a single blanket exemption: U.S. federal tax law offers layered relief, including interim reliance rules in Notices 2023-63 and 2024-12, automatic accounting method changes, new Section 174A domestic expensing, and retroactive elections letting small businesses with average gross receipts up to $31 million unwind 2022–2024 capitalization.
Executive Thesis: The Architecture of Section 174 Safe Harbors

Is there a safe harbor for Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 174 research and experimental (R&E) expenses? Rather than a single blanket exemption, federal tax law in the United States of America provides a multi-layered framework of substantive interim reliance rules, automatic accounting method change procedures, and statutory transition elections.
1. The TCJA Section 174 Capitalization Regime and Interim IRS Safe Harbors
1.1 Mandatory Amortization and Decoupling from ASC 730 (Taxable Years Beginning 2022–2024)

Under Public Law 115-97, 131 Stat. 2054 (enacted December 22, 2017)—commonly known as the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), Section 13206(a)—Congress eliminated the historical option to immediately deduct research and experimental (R&E) expenditures for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Instead, IRC Section 174 mandated that taxpayers capitalize Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures and amortize them ratably over 5 years for domestic research and 15 years for foreign research (defined by reference to IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F) as research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any territory or other possession of the United States), beginning at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenses were paid or incurred.

Analysis and Financial Reporting Mechanics: Under ASC 730, most research and development costs are expensed as incurred for GAAP financial statement purposes because the future economic benefits of early-stage research are uncertain. By requiring 5-year or 15-year tax amortization with a mid-year convention (resulting in only a 10 percent deduction in Year 1 for domestic research and a 3.33 percent deduction in Year 1 for foreign research), TCJA Section 174 created significant book-to-tax timing differences, complex Schedule M-1/M-3 adjustments, deferred tax asset (DTA) reconciliations under ASC 740, and severe cash-flow pressures for research-intensive businesses operating at a book loss (Grant Thornton; LaPorte CPAs).
1.2 Software Development Costs and Partial Obsoletion of Rev. Proc. 2000-50

Under IRC Section 174(c)(3), any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software is explicitly treated as a research or experimental expenditure. Prior to the effective date of the TCJA amendments, taxpayers relied extensively on the administrative safe harbors of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 (2000-2 C.B. 601), which permitted taxpayers to treat the costs of developing computer software in a manner similar to pre-TCJA Section 174—either deducting software development costs currently or capitalizing and amortizing them over 60 months from the date of completion or 36 months from the date the software was placed in service.

items: Statutory and Administrative Precision on Rev. Proc. 2000-50: While broad commentary often asserts that TCJA Section 174(c)(3) formally obsoleted the entirety of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 for tax years beginning after 2021, IRS Notice 2024-12 (Section 5, clarifying Section 12 of Notice 2023-63) and Rev. Proc. 2024-9 specify that only Section 5 of Rev. Proc. 2000-50 (governing the costs of developing computer software) is obsoleted for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Section 5 of Rev. Proc. 2000-50 continues to apply to software development amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning on or before December 31, 2021. Furthermore, the remainder of Rev. Proc. 2000-50—specifically Section 6 (governing the costs of acquired computer software, which are generally capitalized and depreciated over 36 months under IRC Section 167(f)(1)) and Section 7 (governing leased or licensed computer software deductible under Treasury Regulations Section 1.162-11)—was not obsoleted by Section 174(c)(3) and remains in force.

body.text: 1.3 The Section 174(d) Disposition and Abandonment Rule

To prevent taxpayers from accelerating deductions by abandoning or writing off unsuccessful research projects or retired software modules, the TCJA enacted IRC Section 174(d). Under Section 174(d), if any property with respect to which Specified Research or Experimental expenditures are paid or incurred is disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the amortization period, no deduction or reduction to the amount realized is allowed on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment; instead, such amortization deduction must continue over the remainder of the statutory 5-year or 15-year amortization period.

Section 70302(b)(1)(C) of Public Law 119-21—the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA)—subsequently amended Section 174(d) to restrict this disposition, retirement, and abandonment continuation rule exclusively to foreign research or experimental expenditures for property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025, aligning with the restoration of domestic expensing under IRC Section 174A.
1.4 Substantive Reliance Safe Harbors: Notice 2023-63 and Notice 2024-12

To address widespread interpretive ambiguities under TCJA Section 174, the Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service issued substantive interim guidance in Notice 2023-63 (2023-39 I.R.B. 919), which was subsequently clarified and modified by Notice 2024-12 (2024-05 I.R.B. 616, released December 22, 2023, and effective for taxable years ending after September 8, 2023). Together, these notices establish a substantive administrative reliance safe harbor for determining which costs constitute SRE expenditures.

A central area of administrative safe harbor relief involves contract research arrangements and the critical distinction between Section 174 capitalization by a contract research provider and the funded research exclusion under the Section 41 R&D tax credit:

items: Section 41 Funded Research Exclusion: Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulations Section 1.41-4A(d) (as analyzed in IRS Memorandum 20223401F and IRS Memorandum 121401F), a taxpayer performing research for another person under a contract, grant, or sub-agreement cannot claim the Section 41 R&D credit unless the researcher satisfies a conjunctive two-prong test: the researcher must both (1) bear the financial risk of failure (meaning payment is contingent on the technical success of the research rather than paid on a time-and-materials or unconditional milestone basis) and (2) retain substantial rights in the research results.

Section 174 Contract Research Provider Safe Harbor: Conversely, for purposes of determining whether a contract research provider must capitalize its fulfillment costs under Section 174, Notice 2024-12 (Section 3, clarifying Section 6.04 of Notice 2023-63) establishes a disjunctive safe harbor. Costs paid or incurred by a research provider in performing research activities under contract are treated as SRE expenditures subject to Section 174 capitalization only if the research provider either (1) bears financial risk under the terms of the contract, or (2) has a right to use any resulting SRE product in its trade or business or otherwise exploit any resulting SRE product through sale, lease, or license. If the provider bears neither financial risk nor a qualifying right to use or exploit the resulting SRE product, the provider's fulfillment costs are ordinary and necessary business expenses deductible under IRC Section 162 rather than capitalized SRE expenditures.

Clarification on Excluded SRE Product Rights: Notice 2024-12 specifically protects contract researchers from inadvertent Section 174 capitalization by carving out "excluded SRE product rights." If a research provider does not bear financial risk under the contract and obtains only an "excluded SRE product right"—defined as an SRE product right that (a) is separately bargained for (i.e., a right that arose from consideration other than the cost paid or incurred by the research provider to perform SRE activities) or (b) was acquired for the limited purpose of performing SRE activities under that contract or another contract with the research recipient—the provider is not treated as holding a right to use or exploit the SRE product, and its contract fulfillment costs remain exempt from Section 174 capitalization (Grant Thornton).

Selective Reliance Modification: Originally, Section 10.01 of Notice 2023-63 required taxpayers wishing to rely on the interim guidance to apply all rules in Sections 3 through 9 of the notice on an "all-or-nothing" basis. Notice 2024-12 (Section 4, modifying Section 10.01 of Notice 2023-63) eliminated this requirement, allowing taxpayers to rely selectively on specific sections of Notice 2023-63 without being forced to adopt every provision, provided they apply the selected rules consistently (except that taxpayers may not rely on Section 7 of Notice 2023-63 for SRE expenditures relating to property contributed to, distributed from, or transferred from a partnership).

body.text: 1.5 Procedural Accounting Method Safe Harbors: Rev. Proc. 2024-9 and Rev. Proc. 2025-8

Because a change in the treatment of R&E expenditures to comply with TCJA Section 174 or interim IRS guidance constitutes a change in method of accounting under IRC Section 446(e), the IRS established automatic accounting method change safe harbors modifying the List of Automatic Changes in Rev. Proc. 2023-24 and Rev. Proc. 2024-23:

items: Designated Change Number (DCN) 265, DCN 270, and DCN 271 under Rev. Proc. 2024-9: Issued concurrently with Notice 2024-12 on December 22, 2023, Rev. Proc. 2024-9 (2024-05 I.R.B. 628) modified Section 7 of Rev. Proc. 2023-24. While retaining DCN 265 for statutory compliance with TCJA Section 174, Rev. Proc. 2024-9 created DCN 270, granting taxpayers automatic consent to change their method of accounting for expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, to rely on the interim guidance in Sections 3 through 7 of Notice 2023-63, as modified by Notice 2024-12 (and DCN 271 for percentage-of-completion method long-term contracts under Section 460). Crucially, Rev. Proc. 2024-9 clarified that these automatic changes also encompass reclassifying expenditures erroneously treated as SRE expenditures in a prior post-2021 year back to their proper Code provisions (such as IRC Section 162), with the option to implement the change using either a modified IRC Section 481(a) adjustment or a cut-off basis when the modified Section 481(a) adjustment would be negative (Grant Thornton).

Waiver of Eligibility Rules under Rev. Proc. 2025-8: Released on December 17, 2024, Rev. Proc. 2025-8 (2025-03 I.R.B. 427) modified Section 7.01 of Rev. Proc. 2024-23 by extending the waiver of the eligibility restrictions of Section 5.01(1)(d) (final year of a trade or business) and Section 5.01(1)(f) (the prior five-year change restriction for the same item) of Rev. Proc. 2015-13. Under Section 3 of Rev. Proc. 2025-8, taxpayers were permitted to make successive automatic accounting method changes for Section 174 compliance (under DCN 265 or DCN 270) for any taxable year beginning in 2022, 2023, or 2024, regardless of whether the taxpayer had already made an accounting method change for the same item in a previous taxable year beginning in 2022, 2023, or 2024. Additionally, Section 5.02 of Rev. Proc. 2025-8 allowed taxpayers with pending non-automatic Forms 3115 for 2024 to convert them to automatic changes and recover their user fees if notification was submitted by the later of January 17, 2025, or the issuance of a letter ruling.
Precision Analysis of Audit Protection under Rev. Proc. 2025-8:

Pre-2022 Expenditures and Delinquent 2022–2023 Filers: First, audit protection under Section 8.01 of Rev. Proc. 2015-13 is explicitly denied with respect to expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning on or before December 31, 2021. Second, for accounting method changes made for a taxable year beginning in 2022 or 2023 (specifically, the second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021), audit protection is denied if the taxpayer failed to make (or attempt to make) a Section 174 accounting method change for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021.

Restoration of Standard Audit Protection for 2024 Method Changes: Crucially, Rev. Proc. 2025-8 did not extend the 2022/2023 audit protection prohibition to taxable years beginning in 2024. Consequently, a taxpayer filing an automatic Form 3115 for a taxable year beginning in 2024 under Rev. Proc. 2025-8 receives standard Section 8.01 audit protection for post-2021 taxable years (assuming it otherwise qualifies under Rev. Proc. 2015-13), even if the taxpayer failed to file a Section 174 accounting method change in its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021 (BDO USA).

body.text: 2. The One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) and Retroactive Small Business Safe Harbors
2.1 Enactment of IRC Section 174A and the Domestic vs. Foreign Split

On July 4, 2025, Public Law 119-21, 139 Stat. 72—commonly known as the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA)—was enacted into law (Rev. Proc. 2025-28, Section 1). Under Section 70302 of the OBBBA, Congress enacted IRC Section 174A, which permanently restores the option for taxpayers to immediately deduct domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Alternatively, under IRC Section 174A(c), a taxpayer may elect to charge domestic research or experimental expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months, beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures.

However, the OBBBA retained mandatory capitalization and 15-year amortization under amended IRC Section 174 for foreign research or experimental expenditures (research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any territory or other possession of the United States within the meaning of Section 41(d)(4)(F)), along with the Section 174(d) disposition, retirement, and abandonment restrictions for foreign research property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025 (Rev. Proc. 2025-28, Section 2.02).
2.2 Retroactive Small Business Elections under Rev. Proc. 2025-28 and Rev. Proc. 2026-32

Under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(1) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (released August 28, 2025; published September 15, 2025, in 2025-38 I.R.B. 393, and subsequently modified by Rev. Proc. 2026-32, released September 4, 2026, in 2026-39 I.R.B.), Congress and the IRS established a comprehensive retroactive safe harbor allowing eligible small business taxpayers to unwind TCJA domestic capitalization for the 2022, 2023, and 2024 taxable years:

items: Small Business Gross Receipts Threshold ($31,000,000 Test): Under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(1)(B) and Sections 2.08 and 3 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, an "eligible small business taxpayer" is defined as any taxpayer (other than a tax shelter prohibited from using the cash method under IRC Section 448(a)(3) and Section 448(d)(3)) that meets the gross receipts test of IRC Section 448(c) for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024. For a taxable year beginning in 2025, the inflation-adjusted Section 448(c) threshold requires that the taxpayer's average annual gross receipts for the three prior taxable years (i.e., the 2022, 2023, and 2024 taxable years for a calendar-year taxpayer, aggregated across related entities under Section 448(c)(2)) do not exceed $31,000,000. (This clarifies shorthand descriptions suggesting the $31,000,000 cap applies separately to each individual year from 2022 through 2024; legally, it is a single three-prior-year average tested in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024.)

Pathway 1 — Retroactive Amended Returns or AARs (Section 3.03 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28): An eligible small business taxpayer may elect under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(1) to apply the amendments of OBBBA Section 70302 (including immediate domestic expensing under Section 174A) retroactively to amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025 (the 2022–2024 window). Under Section 3.03 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, the taxpayer executes this election by filing amended federal income tax returns (or Administrative Adjustment Requests (AARs) for BBA partnerships under IRC Section 6227) for each applicable taxable year, attaching an election statement titled "FILED PURSUANT TO SECTION 3.03 OF REV. PROC. 2025-28" containing the taxpayer's identification details and election declarations. Under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(1)(C), this election must be made on or before July 6, 2026 (one year after OBBBA enactment, adjusted for the weekend/holiday rule under IRC Section 7503), or such later window permitted by IRS administrative procedures.

Pathway 2 — Automatic Accounting Method Change and IRC Section 481(a) Adjustment (Section 7 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 and Rev. Proc. 2026-32): Recognizing the administrative burden of amending up to three years of federal and state tax returns, the IRS created an alternative procedural safe harbor in Section 7 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (modifying Section 7.01 of Rev. Proc. 2025-23, and further refined by Rev. Proc. 2026-32). Rather than filing amended returns or AARs for 2022, 2023, and 2024, an eligible small business making the OBBBA Section 70302(f)(1) election may implement the retroactive application of Section 174A through an automatic change in method of accounting, computing a Section 481(a) adjustment that deducts or recovers the remaining unamortized domestic R&E costs without amending prior-year tax returns.

General Transition Election for All Taxpayers (OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2)): In addition to the small business retroactive election under Section 70302(f)(1), OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2) and Section 7.02 of Rev. Proc. 2025-23 (as modified by Rev. Proc. 2025-28) permit any taxpayer (regardless of gross receipts) with unamortized domestic SRE expenditures capitalized in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, to make an automatic accounting method change to deduct the remaining unamortized domestic balance either (a) in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or (b) ratably over the two-taxable-year period beginning with the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024.

body.text: 2.3 The Section 280C(c)(2) Late Election and Revocation Safe Harbor

Retroactively deducting domestic R&E expenses under Section 174A directly alters the interaction between research deductions and the Section 41 R&D tax credit under IRC Section 280C(c). During the 2022–2024 TCJA window, Section 280C(c)(1) required a taxpayer to reduce its capitalized domestic SRE amount only to the extent that the Section 41 credit exceeded the current-year Section 174 amortization deduction—meaning most taxpayers did not need to elect the reduced credit under Section 280C(c)(2) to preserve their deduction. However, under OBBBA's retroactive restoration of Section 174A and amended Section 280C(c)(1), a taxpayer claiming the full Section 41 research credit must reduce its domestic Section 174A deduction (or capital account) dollar-for-dollar by the full amount of the research credit, unless the taxpayer makes an election under IRC Section 280C(c)(2) to claim a reduced credit (reduced by the maximum corporate tax rate of 21 percent, yielding a net credit of 79 percent of the gross credit) (IRS Instructions for Form 6765).

items: Late Section 280C(c)(2) Elections, Revocations, and the September 15, 2025 Cutoff Date: Although IRC Section 280C(c)(2)(C) statutorily requires the reduced-credit election to be made on a timely filed original return, Sections 4 and 5 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 establish a vital administrative safe harbor: an eligible small business taxpayer applying OBBBA Section 70302(f)(1) retroactively is permitted to make a late election under Section 280C(c)(2) (under Section 4 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28) or revoke a prior Section 280C(c)(2) election (under Section 5 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28) for any applicable 2022–2024 taxable year on an amended return or AAR, independently for each prior year. Furthermore, September 15, 2025 (the official Internal Revenue Bulletin publication date of Rev. Proc. 2025-28) serves two distinct operational functions in the revenue procedure:

Under Section 3.03 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, for an applicable taxable year whose original federal income tax return was filed on or before September 15, 2025, a pass-through small business may disregard the additional deductions generated by the retroactive Section 3.03 election when determining whether it allocates more than 35 percent of its losses to limited entrepreneurs or limited partners—preventing the retroactive R&E deduction itself from inadvertently converting the business into a "syndicate" or "tax shelter" under IRC Section 448(d)(3) and Section 1256(e)(3)(B).

Under Section 8 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, calendar-year and fiscal-year entities whose 2024 original federal income tax return due date (excluding extensions) fell before September 15, 2025, and who filed a timely return without extension, were granted an automatic six-month extension of time to file a superseding 2024 return to apply OBBBA Section 70302 and Rev. Proc. 2025-28.

body.text: 4. Hypothetical Worked Examples: Section 174/174A Safe Harbors in Practice
4.1 Hypothetical Example 1: Small Business Retroactive Section 174A Recovery and Late Section 280C(c)(2) Election under Rev. Proc. 2025-28

items: Hypothetical Facts: Assume "Apex Robotics Inc." is a calendar-year U.S. C corporation (not a tax shelter under Section 448(d)(3)) with annual gross receipts of $24,000,000 in 2022, $28,000,000 in 2023, and $32,000,000 in 2024. In each of 2022, 2023, and 2024, Apex paid $1,000,000 in domestic SRE expenditures (and $0 in foreign SRE expenditures), which it properly capitalized and amortized over 5 years using the mid-year convention under TCJA Section 174. Assume Apex claimed a $100,000 gross regular Section 41 credit in 2022 on its timely filed original return before September 15, 2025, without making a Section 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election (because its $100,000 credit did not exceed its $100,000 Year 1 amortization deduction under the TCJA version of Section 280C(c)(1)).
Step 1 — Verify Section 448(c) Small Business Eligibility:
Sum of gross receipts for the three prior taxable years (2022–2024): $24,000,000 + $28,000,000 + $32,000,000 = $84,000,000.
Average annual gross receipts for 2022–2024 tested in the 2025 taxable year: $84,000,000 / 3 = $28,000,000.

Because $28,000,000 is less than or equal to the $31,000,000 inflation-adjusted threshold for a taxable year beginning in 2025 (Rev. Proc. 2025-28, Section 2.08), Apex qualifies as an eligible small business taxpayer even though its 2024 gross receipts ($32,000,000) exceeded $31,000,000 in isolation.
Step 2 — Calculate Unamortized Domestic SRE Balance as of December 31, 2024 (Before Retroactive Election):

2022 Cohort ($1,000,000): 10% deducted in 2022 ($100,000); 20% deducted in 2023 ($200,000); 20% deducted in 2024 ($200,000). Total deducted through 2024 = $500,000. Remaining unamortized balance = $1,000,000 - $500,000 = $500,000.
2023 Cohort ($1,000,000): 10% deducted in 2023 ($100,000); 20% deducted in 2024 ($200,000). Total deducted through 2024 = $300,000. Remaining unamortized balance = $1,000,000 - $300,000 = $700,000.
2024 Cohort ($1,000,000): 10% deducted in 2024 ($100,000). Total deducted through 2024 = $100,000. Remaining unamortized balance = $1,000,000 - $100,000 = $900,000.
Total Unamortized Domestic SRE Balance at End of 2024: $500,000 + $700,000 + $900,000 = $2,100,000.
Step 3 — Compare Procedural Pathways under Rev. Proc. 2025-28:

Pathway A (Amended Returns under Section 3.03): Apex files Forms 1120-X for 2022, 2023, and 2024 with the required Section 3.03 statement to deduct the full $1,000,000 of domestic R&E in each year (increasing net R&E deductions by $900,000 in 2022, $700,000 in 2023, and $500,000 in 2024, totaling $2,100,000). Under Section 4 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, Apex also attaches a late Section 280C(c)(2) election statement to its 2022 Form 1120-X: instead of reducing its restored $1,000,000 Section 174A deduction by the $100,000 gross research credit under amended Section 280C(c)(1), Apex retains the full $1,000,000 deduction and reduces its 2022 research credit by the maximum corporate tax rate of 21% (reducing the $100,000 credit by $21,000 to $79,000, corresponding to the 15.8% reduced regular credit rate versus the 20% gross rate on Form 6765).

Pathway B (Automatic Accounting Method Change under Section 7.01): Instead of amending its 2022, 2023, and 2024 tax returns, Apex files an automatic Form 3115 under Section 7.01 of Rev. Proc. 2025-23 (as modified by Rev. Proc. 2025-28 and Rev. Proc. 2026-32) to take the $2,100,000 negative Section 481(a) adjustment into account without reopening prior-year returns.

body.text: 4.2 Hypothetical Example 2: Dual-Function Software Safe Harbor under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)

items: Hypothetical Facts: Assume "CloudLogistics Corp." spends $800,000 in calendar year 2025 developing a new cloud software platform in the United States. Of that $800,000, $500,000 consists of direct wages and cloud computing supplies attributable to a "dual-function computer software" subset that both manages internal warehouse accounting and allows third-party retail customers to track inventory orders. After isolating purely internal-use elements ($100,000) and purely third-party elements ($0), the remaining unsegregated dual-function subset incurs $400,000 of otherwise eligible QREs. CloudLogistics reasonably estimates at the start of development that third-party customers will account for 15% of the dual-function subset's total use, and the third-party functionality satisfies the three-part "high threshold of innovation" test.

Step 1 — Section 174A / Section 174 Treatment: Under IRC Section 174(c)(3) and OBBBA Section 174A, all $800,000 of domestic software development costs qualify as domestic R&E expenditures eligible for 100% immediate expensing in 2025, regardless of whether the software is for internal use or third-party use.

Step 2 — Section 41 Dual-Function Safe Harbor Calculation: Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi), because the third-party subset satisfies the high threshold of innovation test and third-party use is reasonably estimated to be at least 10% of the dual-function subset's total use (here, 15% is greater than or equal to 10%), CloudLogistics may apply the regulatory safe harbor to include 25% of the remaining dual-function subset's QREs in its Section 41 credit computation:
Safe Harbor QREs = $400,000 * 25% = $100,000.

body.text: 5. Cost Segregation, Software Segmentation, and Specialized Compliance Architecture
5.1 Structural Divergence Between Section 174/174A SREs and Section 41 QREs

items: Broader Section 174/174A Scope: Encompasses direct research wages, supplies, overhead and indirect costs incident to research (such as utilities, laboratory/facility depreciation, rent, and patent prosecution and attorney fees under 26 CFR § 1.174-2), 100 percent of qualifying contract research where the taxpayer bears risk or holds exploitation rights, all software development costs under Section 174(c)(3), and foreign R&E (which must still be strictly segregated from domestic R&E and capitalized over 15 years under amended Section 174). Furthermore, state and local tax (SALT) non-conformity requires separate multi-state ledger tracking in jurisdictions that decouple from federal TCJA capitalization or fail to conform automatically to OBBBA Section 174A immediate expensing (Perkins & Co).

Narrower Section 41 QRE Scope and the Four-Part Test: Restricted strictly to domestic research wages (excluding nontaxable fringe benefits), supplies consumed in research, computer rental or cloud hosting used directly in research, and 65 percent (or 75 percent / 100 percent for qualified research consortia and eligible energy research) of qualifying contract research, with zero overhead, indirect facility costs, or patent legal fees permitted. To qualify under IRC Section 41(d), each business component activity must satisfy the statutory four-part test:
Section 174 Test: Expenditures must qualify as research or experimental expenditures eligible under Section 174 (or Section 174A).

Technological in Nature Test: The activity must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, fundamentally relying on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

Permitted Purpose / Elimination of Uncertainty Test: The application of that technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention), specifically seeking to eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving the component's function, performance, reliability, or quality.

Process of Experimentation Test: Substantially all (at least 80 percent under Treasury Regulations Section 1.41-4(a)(6)) of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation involving the identification of uncertainty, evaluation of one or more alternatives, and systematic modeling, simulation, or trial-and-error testing.

body.text: 5.2 Internal Use Software (IUS) and the Dual-Function Safe Harbor

While all software development costs fall within Section 174(c)(3) for deduction or capitalization purposes, software developed primarily for internal use—defined under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6) and Treasury Decision 9786 (IRB 2016-42) as software developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer for use in general and administrative functions (specifically financial management, human resources management, and support services) that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business—is excluded from the Section 41 credit unless it satisfies an additional three-part high threshold of innovation test:

items: The software is innovative (intended to result in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable operating improvement that is substantial and economically significant, if development is successful);

The software development involves significant economic risk (the taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period); and

The software is not commercially available for use by the taxpayer (cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would themselves satisfy the first two requirements).

body.text: Where software is presumed or determined to serve both general/administrative functions and third-party interactions ("dual-function computer software"), 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi) provides an administrative safe harbor: after using reasonable criteria to isolate exclusively internal-use and exclusively third-party subsets, a taxpayer may include 25 percent of the QREs of the remaining dual-function subset in computing the Section 41 credit, provided that the third-party subset satisfies the three-part high threshold of innovation test and third-party use is reasonably estimated at the beginning of development to constitute at least 10 percent of the dual-function subset's total use.
